stem.en: Under perfect competition, a firm is a:

explanation.en: With a very large number of sellers of a homogeneous product, no single firm can influence the market price; it accepts it.

stem.en: Which is NOT a feature of perfect competition?

options.en: Large number of buyers and sellers

explanation.en: Products are identical and information is perfect, so there is no need for advertisement.

stem.en: Free entry and exit of firms ensures that in the long run firms earn:

explanation.en: Profits attract new firms and losses drive firms out until price equals minimum average cost: only normal profit remains.

stem.en: Under perfect competition, the demand curve facing an individual firm is:

explanation.en: The firm can sell any quantity at the market price, so its demand curve is a horizontal line at that price.

stem.en: If a perfectly competitive firm charges a price higher than the market price, it will:

explanation.en: Buyers have perfect information and identical products are available elsewhere at the market price, so it sells nothing.

stem.en: For a perfectly competitive firm, which relation is true?

explanation.en: Each extra unit sells at the same price, so AR = MR = p.

stem.en: A firm sells 50 units at ₹12 each in a perfectly competitive market. Its total revenue is:
The TR curve of a perfectly competitive firm is:

options.en: an upward-sloping straight line from the origin

explanation.en: TR = p × q with p constant, so TR is a straight line from the origin with slope p.

stem.en: The slope of the TR curve of a price-taking firm equals:

explanation.en: Slope of TR = ΔTR/Δq = MR = p.

stem.en: If the market price rises from ₹10 to ₹15, the price line (AR = MR) of a competitive firm:

explanation.en: The firm's horizontal demand (AR = MR) line is at the market price, so it shifts up to ₹15. The TR line becomes steeper.

stem.en: A perfectly competitive firm maximises profit where:

options.en: p = MC and MC is rising

explanation.en: At the profit-maximising output, price equals marginal cost and MC is non-decreasing at that output.

stem.en: Profit of a firm is:

explanation.en: Profit π = total revenue − total cost.

stem.en: Price is ₹12. TC for 0 to 6 units is ₹10, 15, 18, 22, 28, 38, 52. The profit-maximising output is:

explanation.en: Profit = 12q − TC: −10, −3, 6, 14, 20, 22, 20. Maximum ₹22 at 5 units (MC of the 6th unit, 14, exceeds 12).

stem.en: If at the current output price exceeds MC, a profit-maximising competitive firm should:

explanation.en: An extra unit adds more to revenue (p) than to cost (MC), so increasing output raises profit.

stem.en: Why must MC be rising (not falling) at the profit-maximising output?

options.en: Because where MC is falling, producing a little more adds more to revenue than to cost

explanation.en: If p = MC where MC is falling, MC goes below p for the next units, so producing more would raise profit: that point is not a maximum.

stem.en: The short-run supply curve of a competitive firm is:

options.en: the rising part of SMC above minimum AVC
the rising part of SMC below minimum AVC

explanation.en: The firm produces where p = SMC only if p ≥ minimum AVC; below that it shuts down.

stem.en: The shut-down point of a firm in the short run is where price equals:

explanation.en: Below minimum AVC the firm cannot even cover variable cost and loses less by shutting down (its loss is then only TFC).

stem.en: The break-even point is the point where:

explanation.en: At p = minimum AC, TR = TC and the firm earns just normal profit (zero economic profit).

stem.en: Normal profit is:

options.en: the minimum profit needed to keep a firm in the industry

explanation.en: Normal profit is the minimum return needed to keep the firm in business; it is included in costs, so at break-even economic profit is zero.

stem.en: A firm has TFC = ₹30, minimum AVC = ₹12 and minimum AC = ₹20. If the market price is ₹15, in the short run the firm will:

options.en: produce, making a loss smaller than ₹30

explanation.en: Price ₹15 lies between min AVC (₹12) and min AC (₹20): the firm covers variable cost and part of fixed cost, so producing loses less than shutting down (₹30).

stem.en: An improvement in technology will shift a firm's supply curve:

explanation.en: Better technology lowers marginal cost, so the firm supplies more at every price: supply shifts right.

stem.en: Imposition of a unit tax on a good shifts the firm's supply curve:

explanation.en: A unit tax raises marginal cost by the tax at every output, so less is supplied at each price.

stem.en: The market supply curve is obtained by:

options.en: vertical summation of firms' supply curves
horizontal summation of firms' supply curves

explanation.en: At each price, add the quantities supplied by all firms.

stem.en: A rise in the price of an input (say, wages) causes:

options.en: a rightward shift of the supply curve
a movement along the supply curve
a leftward shift of the supply curve

explanation.en: Higher input prices raise costs, so the firm supplies less at each price.

stem.en: Firm 1 supplies s₁ = p − 10 (p ≥ 10) and firm 2 supplies s₂ = p − 15 (p ≥ 15). Market supply at p = ₹20 is:

explanation.en: s₁ = 20 − 10 = 10, s₂ = 20 − 15 = 5; market supply = 15 units.

stem.en: Price rises from ₹10 to ₹12 and quantity supplied rises from 200 to 250 units. The price elasticity of supply is:
A straight-line supply curve passing through the origin has elasticity:

explanation.en: For q = dp, eS = (dq/dp)(p/q) = d × p/(dp) = 1 at every point.

stem.en: A straight-line supply curve that meets the price axis (positive price intercept) has elasticity:

explanation.en: If q = c + dp with c < 0 (price intercept positive), eS = dp/(c + dp) > 1.

stem.en: A vertical supply curve shows that supply is:

explanation.en: Quantity supplied stays the same at every price: eS = 0.

stem.en: For the supply curve q = 10 + 2p, the price elasticity of supply at p = ₹5 is:

explanation.en: q = 10 + 10 = 20. eS = 2 × 5/20 = 0.5 (supply curve meets the quantity axis, so eS < 1).

stem.en:
Assertion (A): In the short run a competitive firm may continue production even when it makes a loss.
Reason (R): As long as price covers average variable cost, the loss from producing is not greater than total fixed cost.

options.en: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation.en: Both true and R explains A: if p ≥ min AVC, producing covers variable cost and part of fixed cost, so the loss is less than (or equal to) TFC, the loss from shutting down.

stem.en:
Assertion (A): For a perfectly competitive firm, the AR curve and the MR curve are the same horizontal line.
Reason (R): A perfectly competitive firm can sell more only by lowering its price.

options.en: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation.en: A is true. R is false: a competitive firm can sell any quantity at the market price; it need not lower its price.

stem.en: How many crates per hour should Lakshmi produce to maximise profit?

explanation.en: Profit = 12q − TC = −10, −3, 6, 14, 20, 22, 20; maximum (₹22) at 5 crates, where MC (10) ≤ 12 and the next unit's MC (14) > 12.

passage.en: Lakshmi grows tomatoes near Kolar and sells them at the APMC market, where thousands of farmers sell identical tomatoes and the price is ₹12 per crate. Her total cost of producing 0 to 6 crates per hour (including the normal profit she expects) is ₹10, 15, 18, 22, 28, 38 and 52.

stem.en: Why can Lakshmi not sell her tomatoes at ₹14 a crate?

options.en: Because the government fixes the price at ₹12
Because she is a price taker: buyers can get identical tomatoes from other farmers at ₹12
Because demand for tomatoes is perfectly inelastic

explanation.en: With many sellers of an identical product and well-informed buyers, a single seller asking more than the market price sells nothing.

passage.en: Lakshmi grows tomatoes near Kolar and sells them at the APMC market, where thousands of farmers sell identical tomatoes and the price is ₹12 per crate. Her total cost of producing 0 to 6 crates per hour (including the normal profit she expects) is ₹10, 15, 18, 22, 28, 38 and 52.

stem.en: For a competitive firm, match: (a) p = min AVC (b) p = min AC (c) p > min AC (d) p < min AVC with (i) super-normal profit (ii) shut down (iii) shut-down point (iv) break-even point

explanation.en: Min AVC is the shut-down point, min AC the break-even point; above min AC the firm earns super-normal profit; below min AVC it shuts down.

stem.en: A competitive firm has MC = 10 − 4q + 0.75q². If the market price is ₹13, its profit-maximising output is:

explanation.en: Set p = MC on the rising part: 0.75q² − 4q − 3 = 0 → q = (4 + √(16 + 9))/1.5 = (4 + 5)/1.5 = 6. (The other root is negative.)

stem.en: Which of the following makes the supply of a good more price-elastic?

options.en: A longer time period for producers to adjust

explanation.en: Over a longer period firms can change inputs and capacity, so quantity supplied responds more to price.
